answer: A micro-batch engine's latency floor is the trigger plus the run time, and each cycle pays a fixed planning and offset-commit cost of about 1 second. At a 100 ms trigger that overhead dominates almost all of the cycle, so the trigger cannot get you near real time. Below about 1 second the micro-batch model stops paying, and a record-at-a-time engine (10 to 100 ms latency) is what crosses that line. Shrinking the trigger also worsens the tail, since p99 is roughly the trigger plus the slowest run. If your SLA is looser, e.g. 30 s or minutes, a micro-batch trigger on your existing cluster is the better choice, and the team's existing skills decide it.
